column4: ### The Body
column5: ### Body

column4: The church is often described as **the Body of Christ**, emphasizing both its unity and diversity. With Christ as the head, the church functions as a living organism where every believer plays an essential and potentially diverse role. Each member is uniquely gifted and contributes to the health and mission of the body according to their own function. This image highlights the interdependence of believers, specifically that the body must be connected to function, and that our function is collaborative not competitive. When every part works together, the body grows and thrives in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).
column5: The church is often described as the **Body of Christ**, with both its unity and diversity emphasized. With Christ as the head, the church functions as a living organism, and every believer has roles that are indispensable and can be diverse. Each member is given unique gifts and contributes to the body’s health and mission according to their function. This image underscores believers’ mutual interdependence, showing especially that, for the body to function, it must remain connected, and that our work is cooperation, not competition. When all the parts work together, the body grows and thrives in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).

column4: ### The Bride
column5: ### Bride

column4: The church is described as **the Bride of Christ**, this reflects an intimate and loving relationship with Jesus. Just as a bride is cherished and made ready for her husband, the church is sanctified and purified by Christ’s sacrificial love. This metaphor captures the devotion and faithfulness expected of the church, as well as the deep affection Christ has for His people. The imagery also points to the ultimate union between Christ and the church, celebrated in the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the church is presented in glory without spot or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7-9; Revelation 21:2).
column5: The church is portrayed as the **Bride of Christ**, which represents an intimate and loving relationship with Jesus. Just as a bride is cherished and prepared for her husband, the church is sanctified and cleansed by Christ’s sacrificial love. This metaphor captures the devotion and faithfulness required of the church, as well as the profound affection Christ has for His people. This image also points to the final union of Christ and the church, celebrated at the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the church is presented in a glorious state, without spot or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7-9; Revelation 21:2).

column4: ### The Temple
column5: ### Temple

column4: The church is described as **the Temple of God**, the dwelling place of His Spirit. Believers are described as living stones being built together on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone. This holy structure signifies God’s presence among His people and their role as a community of worship and prayer. The temple imagery underscores the importance of holiness and the church’s collective purpose in glorifying God (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5).
column5: The church is depicted as the **temple of God**, the dwelling place of the Spirit. Believers, as living stones, are being built together on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone. This holy structure signifies God’s presence in the midst of His people and their role as a community of worship and prayer. The image of the temple underscores the importance of holiness and the church’s shared purpose of manifesting God’s glory (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5).

column4: ### The Family
column5: ### Family

column4: The church is described as **the Family of God**, emphasizing relational unity and care among its members. Through the Spirit of adoption, believers are made children of God and members of His household. This familial imagery highlights the love, belonging, and shared inheritance believers have in Christ. It also reflects the call to treat one another with compassion and humility as brothers and sisters in God’s family (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; Romans 8:15-17). Furthermore, through the family image it depicts how the members of the church are to become mature, that they would be taught and nourished by spiritual mothers and fathers (1 Timothy 5:1-2), that we could go from infants drinking the pure milk of the Word, to full grown adults able to eat the strong meat of the Word (Hebrews 5).
column5: The church is portrayed as the **family of God**, emphasizing relational unity and care among its members. By the Spirit of adoption, believers become children of God and members of God’s household. This family image highlights the love, belonging, and shared inheritance of believers in Christ. It also reflects the call to treat one another with compassion and humility as brothers and sisters in God’s family (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; Romans 8:15-17)。Furthermore, this family image depicts the church’s members moving toward maturity—that is, being taught and nurtured by spiritual fathers and mothers (1 Timothy 5:1-2)、and our progress from infants who drink the pure milk of the word to adults who can eat the solid food of the word（Hebrews 5）。

column4: ### The Flock
column5: ### Flock of sheep

column4: The church is described as **the Flock**, sheep under the care of Jesus, the Good Shepherd. This image conveys the church’s dependence on Christ for guidance, sustenance, and protection. It also emphasizes the responsibility of church leaders to faithfully shepherd God’s flock as under shepherds, mirroring Christ’s example of love and care. The flock imagery speaks to trust, obedience, and the close relationship between the Great Shepherd and His sheep (John 10:14-16; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).
column5: The church is depicted as a **flock**, sheep under the care of Jesus, the Good Shepherd. This image conveys the church’s dependence on Christ for guidance, nourishment, and protection. It also emphasizes that church leaders, as those under the Shepherd, have the responsibility to faithfully shepherd God’s flock, reflecting Christ’s model of love and care. The image of the flock speaks of trust, obedience, and close relationship between the great Shepherd and His sheep (John 10:14-16; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).

column4: ### The Vine and Branches
column5: ### Vine and branches

column4: The church is described as **the Vine and Branches**, illustrating the essential connection between believers and Christ. Jesus is the true vine, and believers are the branches that must remain in Him to bear fruit. This metaphor highlights dependence on Christ for spiritual vitality, growth, and productivity. Without Him, believers can do nothing, but by abiding in Him, they glorify God and fulfill their purpose. Jesus will prune so that He can bear more fruit in our lives (John 15:1-5).
column5: The church is portrayed as the **vine and branches**, showing the indispensable union between believers and Christ. Jesus is the true vine, and believers are the branches that must abide in Him to bear fruit. This metaphor emphasizes dependence on Christ for spiritual life, growth, and fruitfulness. Apart from Him believers can do nothing, but by abiding in Him they manifest God’s glory and fulfill their purpose. Jesus prunes us so that more fruit may be borne in our lives (John 15:1-5)。

column4: ## Roles of the Church
column5: ## The Role of the Church

column4: The church’s mission, like the Holy Spirit's role, can be understood through three dimensions: upward, inward, and outward, each reflecting a unique aspect of its calling in God’s plan. These dimensions guide the church in fulfilling its role as a worshiping, edifying, and missional community.
column5: The mission of the church, like the role of the Holy Spirit, can be understood in three dimensions: upward, inward, and outward. Each of these reflects a distinct facet of the church’s calling within God’s plan. These dimensions serve as guidelines for the church to fulfill its role as a community that worships, builds up, and witnesses.

column4: ### Upward: Worship and Glorifying God
column5: ### Upward: Worship and Giving Glory to God

column4: The church’s first purpose is to worship and glorify God. Corporate worship, where believers gather to exalt God together, is a visible reflection of His glory and a response to His greatness. As the psalmist declares, “*Worship the Lord in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth*” (Psalms 96:9). Beyond corporate worship, the church is called to live lives of obedience and sacrifice, offering themselves as “living sacrifices” as an act of spiritual worship (Romans 12:1-2). This upward focus keeps the church centered on God’s majesty and aligns its priorities with His will.
column5: The church’s primary purpose is to worship God and give glory to Him. Congregational worship, in which believers gather together to exalt God, visibly reflects His glory and responds to His greatness. As the psalmist declares, “*Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness; all the earth, tremble before Him*” (Psalm 96:9). Beyond congregational worship, the church is called to a life of obedience and sacrifice, and offering ourselves as “living sacrifices” is said to be an act of spiritual worship (Romans 12:1-2). This upward focus keeps the church centered on the majesty of God and continually aligns its priorities with His will.

Jesus’ Great Commission calls His followers to evangelize and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19-20). Empowered by the Holy Spirit, the church is to be His witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

We are the light of the world; our lives we are to radiate His light in our darkened worlds and demonstrate good works that glorify God (Matthew 5:14-16). Practically this means the church is called to advocate for justice and mercy, both spiritual and physical. As James says, our pure worship is to care for the vulnerable, the fatherless, the widow (James 1:27).

column4: ### Church at Jerusalem
column5: ### The Church in Jerusalem

column4: The church at Jerusalem was led primarily by the **apostles**, who focused on teaching, prayer, and spiritual oversight (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4). As the community grew, the need for administrative structure became apparent, particularly to address practical matters like caring for widows and distributing resources. This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7). These individuals, chosen for their spiritual maturity and good reputation, handled practical ministries to allow the apostles to focus on their spiritual responsibilities. Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the Jerusalem church. For instance, during the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), both apostles and elders were involved in decision-making, showing a collaborative leadership structure.
column5: The church in Jerusalem was led primarily by the **apostles**, who devoted themselves to teaching, prayer, and spiritual oversight (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4). As the community grew, the need for an administrative structure became evident to address practical issues such as care for widows and the distribution of resources. This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7). They were chosen for their spiritual maturity and good reputation, and took on practical service so that the apostles could focus on their spiritual responsibilities. Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the church at Jerusalem. For example, at the Jerusalem Council（Acts 15）, both apostles and elders were involved in decision-making, demonstrating a collaborative leadership structure.

column4: ### Church at Antioch
column5: ### The Church in Antioch

column4: The church at Antioch had a more decentralized and diverse leadership structure compared to Jerusalem. It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers**, including Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1). The church at Antioch was also much more oriented towards reaching the gentiles, where the church in Jerusalem reflected more of its Jewish roots. While the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, it is likely that practical roles existed given the church's growing size and involvement in sending relief to Jerusalem (Acts 11:29-30). The church at Antioch became a model for commissioning missionaries, with leaders praying, fasting, and laying hands on Paul and Barnabas to send them out (Acts 13:2-3). This demonstrates a structure that balanced spiritual oversight (prophets and teachers) with missional outreach and practical support.
column5: The church in Antioch had a more decentralized and diverse leadership structure compared to Jerusalem. It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers** that included Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1). The church in Antioch had a strong missionary focus to the Gentiles, whereas the church in Jerusalem reflected more of its Jewish roots. Although the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, given the church’s growth in size and its involvement in sending relief to Jerusalem, it is likely that practical roles existed (Acts 11:29-30). The church in Antioch served as a model in the appointment of missionaries: the leaders prayed, fasted, laid hands on Paul and Barnabas, and sent them out (Acts 13:2-3). This shows a structure that balanced spiritual oversight（prophets and teachers）with missionary work and practical support.

column4: Unlike Paul’s corrections to the Corinthians and Galatians, the scriptures do not critique the leadership structures of Jerusalem or Antioch. This suggests that these churches, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, were free to adapt their gatherings to meet their unique needs and circumstances within the framework of sound doctrine and apostolic teaching (Acts 2:42, 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

This suggests that these churches, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and within the framework of sound doctrine and apostolic teaching, freely adapted their gatherings to their unique needs and circumstances (Acts 2:42, 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

column4: ## Leadership Versus Gifting
column5: ## Leadership and Gifts

column4: A commonly misunderstood aspect of leadership in the church is the separation between the authority and responsibility of leadership, and specific giftings.
column5: What is often misunderstood regarding church leadership is separating leadership authority and responsibility from specific gifts.

column4: This confusion is centered on our use of words like teacher, paster, prophet, apostle, evangelist. These words are gifts. There is not an **office** of ‘apostle’ in the New Testament church. There are people who do the work of an apostle, who have the gift or calling of apostle. Having the gift of apostle does not give them authority of responsibility.
column5: This confusion centers on the way terms like teacher, pastor, prophet, apostle, and evangelist are used. These terms refer to gifts. There is no **office** of 『apostle』 in the New Testament church. There are people who do the work of an apostle and who have an apostolic gift and calling. However, possessing an apostolic gift does not in itself confer authority or responsibility.

column4: I am a skilled musician; I have played saxophone for over 20 years. I played through school and college and played semi-professionally for several summers while working with an evangelistic team. Despite me having the skill, gift, and ability to be a saxophonist, I do not have the right to come into your church and stand on the stage with the worship team.
column5: I am a skilled musician. I have played the saxophone for over 20 years. I played throughout school and college, and while working on an evangelism team, I also played semi-professionally for several summers. Even if I have the skill, gift, and ability as a saxophonist, that does not give me the right to come to your church and take the stage with the worship team.

column4: Likewise, there are people gifted in being a pastor/shepherd, but that does not make them ‘THE PASTOR’ of the local church or make them ‘your’ pastor. The five-fold ministry gifts do not lead the church, the leaders (elders and deacons) do. It is very common for leaders to have specific five-fold ministry gifts, but that gift enhances their leadership, it doesn’t create it. Likewise, it's common for still-developing people with fivefold giftings to serve and aspire to leadership, but God is first interested in character, then interested in giftings. We are all to become mature, able to discern the word of God, full of the spirit, and doing good works.
column5: Similarly, even if someone has a pastoral／shepherding gift, that does not make them the ‘pastor’ of a local church or your ‘pastor’. It is not the fivefold ministry gifts that lead the church, but the leaders (elders and deacons). While leaders often have particular fivefold gifts, those gifts enhance leadership but do not themselves produce leadership. Likewise, it is common for people with developing fivefold gifts to serve and aspire to leadership, but what God is concerned with first is character, and only then gifts. We all should become mature, discern the word of God, be filled with the Spirit, and devote ourselves to good works.

column5: All leaders and all gifts must first submit to being disciples, that is, members of the body.

As disciples grow, the five-fold ministry gifts equip them for ministry, while elders and deacons provide oversight to ensure sound doctrine and practice.

column4: ## Your Role in the Church
column5: ## Your Role in the Church

column4: So far in this chapter we’ve covered the leadership of the church and the core analogies for the church. Let’s build upon the specific analogy of *the body* and consider a marathon runner.
column5: Up to this point in this chapter, we have dealt with church leadership and the primary metaphors for the church. From here, building particularly on the metaphor of the 「body」, let us consider a marathon runner.

column4: ### You Are a Part of the Whole
column5: ### You Are Part of the Whole

column4: The church, as the Body of Christ, depends on every member working together to fulfill its mission. Just as the body cannot function properly if one part is missing, the church needs each believer to actively participate, grow, and serve. Each member of the body has a very important role. To be part of the body means staying connected. A body can survive at diminished capacity without a limb, but the limb itself cannot live when separated from the body. We must be an active part of the church and not become dismembered. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should gather and not forsake the assembly.
column5: As the body of Christ, the church depends on all its members working together to fulfill its mission. Just as a body does not function properly when part of it is missing, the church needs each believer to participate actively, grow, and serve. Each part of the body has a very important role. Being part of the body means remaining connected. A body can survive, though with diminished function, even if it lacks a limb. However, that limb itself cannot live if it is severed from the body. We must remain an active part of the church and not become detached. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should gather and not stop meeting.

column4: To really work and function together you need to fellowship! You need to know others, love others and ideally like others! Build strong relationships and friendships and repair them when they become stressed or injured. When a joint gets injured or inflamed, you need to work to rest and or reset it; so that the joint that’s dislodged doesn’t become broken! A broken and unhealing limb will eventually be separated, and you cannot be part of the body, alone.
column5: To truly work and function together, fellowship is necessary！ We need to know, love, and ideally take delight in others！ Build strong relationships and friendships, and repair them when they become strained or hurt. When a joint is sore or inflamed, it needs rest or adjustment； so that a dislocated joint does not end up broken！ A limb that is broken and does not heal will eventually be removed, and in isolation it cannot remain part of the body.

column4: We don’t all have the same function. Some of us may share the Gospel from a stage, others around a dinner table. But we are ALL called to be ministers of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19). We have all been received into the priesthood of believers (1 Peter 2:9, Revelation 1:6). This means that we're all supposed to be able to do the work of the ministry by the power of the Holy Spirit.
column5: We do not all have the same function. One may preach the gospel from a stage, another may share it around a table. But we are all called to the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19). We are all received into the priesthood of believers (1 Peter 2:9, Revelation 1:6). This means that all of us should be able to carry out works of ministry by the power of the Holy Spirit.

column4: The toes work with the feet, the feet with the ankles, and so on-each part contributing to the overall mission. Marathon runners must train if they want to be able to complete the race. You need to be ready-not just by learning, but by actually practicing what you’ve learned. The church, like a marathon runner, thrives when each member plays their role in unison.
column5: The toe to the foot, the foot to the ankle, and so on- each part contributes to the mission of the whole. A marathoner must train if they want to finish. Preparation is necessary- not only by learning, but by actually putting what is learned into practice. Like a marathoner, the church shows its strength when each member, in unity, fulfills their role.

column4: There are a great number of people in your life that only you can possibly reach. The Pastor can't be the only one trying to shepherd them, and the Evangelist can't be the only one trying to reach them. God wants to use you to reach unbelievers by the power of His Holy Spirit. We all do the work of the ministry; the Holy Spirit helps us.
column5: In your life there are many people whom only you may be able to reach. It should not be only pastors who shepherd them, nor only evangelists who seek to reach them. God desires to use you, by the power of the Holy Spirit, to reach unbelievers. We all do the work of ministry； the Holy Spirit helps us.

column4: ### You Need Training
column5: ### Training Is Necessary

column4: Believers must train and equip for their unique roles in the church, just as a runner strengthens specific muscles for the race. You won’t be successful if you jump into a marathon and haven’t trained, and not all training is equal, you need to be adequately prepared for the race. Jesus has given specific ministry gifts to equip believers, not to do all the work themselves, but to empower every member to serve effectively in their unique roles.
column5: Believers must train and be equipped for their particular role in the church, as a runner strengthens specific muscles for a race. You will not succeed by suddenly entering a marathon without training, and not all training is the same. You need to be adequately prepared for the race. Jesus gave particular gifts of ministry to equip believers. Not so that He Himself would do all the work, but so that each member would be empowered to serve effectively in their unique role.

column4: Training for a marathon will bring about transformation. You need strength and you need to transform. It’s our responsibility to submit ourselves to God and let him transform us in renewal (Romans 12:1-2). Transformation should lead you to maturity, enabling you to bear your own loads and support others. You should be able to bear MUCH fruit. This will be discussed at length in the chapter on sanctification.
column5: Training for a marathon brings change. You need strength, and you also need to be transformed. It is our responsibility to present ourselves to God and allow Him to transform us in renewal (Romans 12:1-2). Change leads you to maturity, enabling you to carry your own load and support others. You should be able to bear much fruit. This will be addressed in detail in the chapter on sanctification.

column4: Training is hard, sometimes it’s uncomfortable. Sometimes the transformation you need to go through you’d much rather skip. But if you want to accomplish the goal, you need to stay on the narrow path. At times, you might need warning, comfort, or support-all offered with patience (1 Thessalonians 5:14).
column5: Training is rigorous and at times uncomfortable. Sometimes you may wish to avoid the changes you must go through. But if you want to reach the goal, you need to stay on the narrow path. At times there is admonition, comfort, or support- all offered with patience (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

column4: Every great marathon runner has a coach to train them, you will need a trainer to help you. Of course, you have the Holy Spirit, but He often relies on His coaches, the mature men and women of God, in the Body of Christ that you are called to work alongside.
column5: Every excellent marathoner has a coach who trains them. You also need trainers who can help you. Of course, you have the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit often works through His coaches- mature men and women of God within the body of Christ with whom you are called to labor.

column4: As individuals we need to submit ourselves first and foremost to God and secondly, in this context, to a body of believers. Submission in the church means honoring godly leadership (Hebrews 13:17) and submitting to one another in humility (Ephesians 5:21).
column5: As an individual, you must first and foremost submit yourself to God, and then, in this context, submit to the gathering of believers. Obedience in the church means honoring godly leadership (Hebrews 13:17) and humbly submitting to one another (Ephesians 5:21).

column4: Submission can be difficult, especially when you have experienced broken trust or failed leadership previously. This does not imply blind obedience or control but reflects a spirit of reverence and cooperation. Worldly submission is demanded by those in authority and can be degrading and lead to resentment. Biblical submission rooted in humility and discernment strengthens the church and fosters accountability. Be willing to listen to guidance and constructive feedback.
column5: Submitting can be difficult, especially if you have previously experienced a breach of trust or failed leadership. This does not mean blind obedience or domination； it expresses a spirit of reverence and cooperation. Worldly obedience is demanded by those in authority and can lead to servility or resentment. Biblical obedience, rooted in humility and discernment, strengthens the church and fosters accountability. Maintain a posture that listens to guidance and constructive feedback.

column4: Now that we’ve set a strong foundation - you a meaningful part of the body but need training - let’s get down to finding where you fit.
column5: A solid foundation has been laid - you are a meaningful member of the body, but training is necessary - so now let’s find where you fit.

column4: ### Finding Where You Fit
column5: ### Finding Your Place

column4: Finding your role in the church involves seeking God’s guidance, understanding your spiritual gifts, and actively engaging with your church community. It is a journey of prayer, exploration, and growth, where you discover how God has uniquely equipped you to contribute to His kingdom. It's very important to note that your role in the church will likely change over time and is not likely to be the same throughout your entire life.

It is very important to note that your role in the church is likely to change over time and is unlikely to remain the same throughout your life.

column5: - Join a welcome team, children’s ministry, or outreach program. Consider leading a discipleship-oriented group for new believers based on this book, *Principles of Faith,* using the discussion questions and end-of-chapter activities to foster dialogue.

column4: - Be open to stepping outside your comfort zone to discover new opportunities.
column5: - Step out of your comfort zone and be open to discovering new opportunities.

column4: - Observe where God works through you and where you feel most effective.
column5: - Observe where God works through you and where you feel most effective.

column4: Practice giving. We can give to the church in many important ways, and we are instructed to do so to accomplish the mission.
column5: Practice giving. We can give to the church in various important ways, and we are taught to do so in order to fulfill the mission.

column4: - Time - we can give our time and volunteer. When we give our time, we use our efforts and our talents. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and increase existing ones.
column5: - Time - We can give our time and serve as volunteers. When we give our time, we use our efforts and gifts. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and develop existing ones.

column4: - Resources - we can give of our resources. Most commonly today this is probably giving financially to the church and to ministries (not just the “institution”, but those in need in the church). Giving money is useful, because the church can buy needed resources with it, but people have given their physical resources beyond money, for example extra homes, clothing, cars, food, building materials, tools, etc. In Acts 4:32-35 we see an example of early believers giving freely, sharing proceeds from sale of extra lands and homes and giving so that ‘none had need’.
column5: - Resources - We can give our resources. The most common today is probably financial giving to the church or ministries (not just the “institution,” but to people in need within the church). Giving is beneficial. The church can purchase necessary supplies with it. However, people have given not only money but also tangible resources such as an extra house, clothing, cars, food, building materials, and tools. Acts 4:32-35 shows an example of the early believers giving generously, selling extra land or houses and sharing the proceeds, so that ‘no one was in need.’

column4: Working alongside others in ministry can reveal your strengths and deepen your understanding of your role. Engage in small groups or church activities to foster connections. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you connect with others and understand the community’s needs.
column5: Engaging in ministry with others reveals your strengths and deepens your understanding of your role. Join small groups and church activities to cultivate connections. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you be connected to others and understand the needs of the community.

column4: #### Step 4 - Get Help!
column5: #### Step 4 - Get help!

column4: Jesus said that in life we would experience trouble! (John 16:33) We are encouraged to not carry the weight of our burdens by ourselves but to cast them on God who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)
column5: Jesus said we would experience trouble in life! (John 16:33) We are encouraged not to keep carrying our burdens alone but to cast them on the God who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)

column4: Sometimes in our journey we may become injured. Marathon runners, even when doing “everything right” can stress their bodies to the point of injury, or they can trip and fall.
column5: We may get hurt along the way. A marathon runner, even when doing “everything right,” can place stress on the body and end up injured, and may also stumble and fall.

column4: Not all ‘falling’ is sin related, but some of it is, not all weakness is ‘our fault’, sometimes others will sin against us. Regardless for the cause of our weakness or injury we are to be restored and healed.
column5: Not every ‘fall’ is related to sin, though sometimes it is. Not every weakness is ‘our fault,’ and at times others sin against us. Whatever the cause of our weaknesses or wounds, we should be restored and healed.

column4: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the vulnerable parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those caught in trespasses (Galatians 6:1).
column5: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the vulnerable parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those who have fallen into wrongdoing (Galatians 6:1).

column4: There is much to say about this topic, and we explore the themes of healing as an overview in the chapter on sanctification.
column5: There is much to be said on this subject, and we will explore the theme of healing in overview in the chapter on sanctification.

column4: #### Step 5 - Be Patient
column5: #### Step 5 - Persevere

column4: Pay attention to confirmation from God and others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and affirmation from those around you. Reflect on where your efforts have borne fruit and listen to feedback about the impact of the ministry. This can help you recognize where you are most effective in serving the Body of Christ.
column5: Pay attention to confirmation from God and from others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and affirmation from the people around you. Look back at where your efforts have borne fruit, and listen to feedback about the impact of your ministry. This will help you discern where you are most effective in serving the body of Christ.

column4: Be patient and trust God’s timing. Discovering your role may take time and involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Trust that God will guide you as you remain faithful and open to His leading. During this time, commit to growth and training by attending workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that equip you for service. Do this with the church, engage with the body of Christ to discover your gifting.
column5: Be patient and trust God’s timing. It takes time to find your role, and it may involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Believe that God will lead you if you remain faithful and open to His guidance. During this season, commit to growth and training by participating in workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that prepare you for service. Do this with your church, and discover your gifts as you engage with the body of Christ.

column4: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution; it is a living, breathing body made up of people like you. By stepping into your role, you contribute to its mission and glorify Christ as its head.
column5: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution but a living body made up of people like you. As you step into your role, you contribute to its mission and bring glory to Christ, the head.
